haughton.why: 23 km impact crater on Devon Island and home of the Haughton-Mars Project, the best-studied Moon/Mars field site. At 75 N it gets long stretches of low sun around the equinoxes.
works: Real impact-crater morphology: rim, terraces, breccia hills
Polar-desert ground with little vegetation
Low sun angles in spring and autumn, long shadows
Existing field-station infrastructure and decades of analog studies
breaks: Target rock is carbonate (dolomite, limestone) and impact breccia, not basalt or anorthosite
Surface is lighter grey but chemically nothing like the lunar highlands
Snow cover outside the short summer can hide the terrain; HLS imagery shows snow still lying in gullies in mid-July, and the low-sun seasons (spring, autumn) are snowier still
Permafrost and running water in summer shape the ground in un-lunar ways
haughton.access: Charter flight from Resolute Bay, Nunavut; summer field season only (July-August). Permits from Nunavut authorities.

sp_crater.why: Cinder cone and lava flow in the San Francisco volcanic field, next to the Black Point lava flow used for NASA Desert RATS rover and EVA tests.
works: Fresh, blocky volcanic terrain with steep cone flanks
Dark basaltic andesite, close in composition to lunar mare basalt
Dry, unvegetated surface
Proven NASA test logistics in the surrounding area
breaks: Mid-latitude: the Sun crosses the 0-5 degree band in minutes, not days
Dark mare-like rock, much darker than the bright south-pole highlands
Volcanic, not impact, terrain
sp_crater.access: About 50 km north of Flagstaff, Arizona. Much of the area is private ranch land, so access needs landowner permission.

meteor_crater.why: 1.2 km simple impact crater, the classic training site for Apollo astronauts and still used for geology training.
works: Fresh simple-crater shape: raised rim, steep walls, ejecta blanket
Bowl-shaped crater similar to small lunar craters
Dry, sparsely vegetated surface
breaks: Target rocks are sandstone and limestone, not basalt or anorthosite
Bright sandstone ejecta is closer in brightness to the highlands than basalt, but it is a different material
Mid-latitude: low sun lasts only minutes each day
Window is mostly flat plain around a single crater, which dilutes the crater's slope signal
meteor_crater.access: Privately owned with a visitor centre off Interstate 40, east of Flagstaff. Crater-floor access needs permission from the owner.

mauna_kea.why: Upper slopes near Hale Pohaku host NASA's in-situ resource utilisation (ISRU) field tests of 2010 and 2012 on volcanic tephra.
works: Basaltic tephra and cinder cones, a good regolith-handling test bed
Little vegetation at altitude
Steep cone flanks give a wide slope range
breaks: Lowest-latitude site (19.8 N): almost no low-sun time at all
Dark basalt, unlike the bright highlands
Thin atmosphere still present; weather, snow on the summit in winter
mauna_kea.access: Road from Hilo to Hale Pohaku. The mountain is sacred to Native Hawaiians and managed by the Maunakea authority; field work needs permits and cultural consultation.

atacama.why: Yungay is one of the driest places on Earth and a standard analog site for robotic and life-detection tests.
works: Hyperarid, almost lifeless soil
Very stable weather and clear skies for testing
Bright, fine-grained surface
breaks: Sediments and salt crusts, not igneous rock
Rounded hills and alluvial valleys shaped by rare water and wind, with no impact craters
Mid-latitude (24 S): short low-sun periods
atacama.access: Road access from Antofagasta, Chile. Easiest logistics of the high-desert sites.

svalbard.why: Bockfjorden's Sverrefjell volcano and hot-spring deposits were used by the AMASE Mars expeditions but have never been scored for lunar low-sun conditions.
works: Basalt with mantle xenoliths, close to mare-type rock
Very high latitude (79.5 N): weeks of low sun around the equinoxes
Sparse vegetation on volcanic slopes
breaks: Dark basalt, unlike the bright highlands
Fjord water covers roughly 20% of the 10 km window (east edge and a strip along the top); flat water reads as 0-degree slope and inflates the flat bins
Polar night in winter and midnight sun in summer, so low sun is seasonal
svalbard.access: Flight to Longyearbyen, then boat to Bockfjorden in summer. Governor of Svalbard rules apply, including polar bear protection.

peary_land.why: Ice-free polar desert at 82.5 N, one of the northernmost bare-ground regions on Earth.
works: Extreme latitude: the longest low-sun seasons among Northern Hemisphere sites
Very dry, nearly unvegetated ground
Large ice-free area
Dissected plateau with mesas, buttes and steep valley walls gives a wide slope range
breaks: Flat-lying sedimentary layers, not basalt or anorthosite; erosional terraces, not impact craters
Snow cover for much of the year
Near the 83 N edge of ASTER GDEM coverage
peary_land.access: Inside Northeast Greenland National Park; access needs a Greenland government permit and charter flights. Very expensive and remote.

dry_valleys.why: The largest ice-free area in Antarctica, with months of low sun each year.
works: Southern high latitude (77.5 S): long low-sun periods, like the lunar south pole
Cold, dry, wind-scoured surface
Dolerite and granite boulder fields, with steep valley walls
breaks: Ice-covered lakes and glacier tongues sit just outside the window, and ridges hold snow patches
Mixed rock types (granite, dolerite, sandstone)
Permafrost and seasonal meltwater
dry_valleys.access: Only through a national Antarctic programme (e.g. US Antarctic Program from McMurdo Station) by helicopter. Specially managed area with strict environmental rules.

holuhraun.why: Fresh basalt lava field from the 2014-15 eruption, at mid-to-high latitude (64.9 N).
works: Very fresh basalt, close to mare composition
Unweathered, unvegetated surface
Low sun for a good part of the day in spring and autumn
breaks: Lava-flow surface, not impact-cratered
Dark basalt, unlike the bright highlands
Snow cover in winter; volcanic gas and weather
holuhraun.access: In Vatnajokull National Park, reached by highland 4x4 tracks open only in summer.

khaybar.why: Large basalt volcanic field in western Saudi Arabia with cones and lava tubes, such as Umm Jirsan.
works: Extensive dry basalt surface
Lava tubes as an analog for lunar shelter and cave exploration
Cinder cones and flows give varied slopes
breaks: Low latitude (25 N): low sun lasts only minutes
Dark basalt, unlike the bright highlands
Volcanic, not impact, terrain
khaybar.access: Road access from Medina or Khaybar town. Tourist visa available; lava tube visits are best arranged with the Saudi Geological Survey.

kamil.why: A pristine 45 m impact crater made by an iron meteorite only a few thousand years ago, among the best-preserved small craters on Earth.
works: Fresh crater with bright and dark ejecta rays, like small fresh lunar craters
Bare, dry desert with no vegetation
Stable, clear weather
breaks: At 45 m across, the crater is only about 1.5 pixels in a 30 m DEM, so the score mostly reflects the flat plain around it
Target rock is sandstone, not basalt or anorthosite
Low latitude (22 N): the Sun crosses 0 to 5 degrees in roughly 20 to 25 minutes
kamil.access: Remote corner of Egypt's Western Desert right on the Sudan border: the crater is about 2 km north of it, and roughly 40% of the 10 km window lies in Sudan. Needs Egyptian military permits and a multi-day 4x4 expedition.

black_desert.why: Hills capped with dark basalt and dolerite over sandstone south of Bahariya Oasis, the most reachable Egyptian site from Cairo.
works: Dark volcanic caps scattered across the surface
Dry, bare desert with isolated hills
Easy access for repeated field tests
breaks: Dark basalt over orange sandstone: patchy brightness, unlike the uniform highlands
Mostly gentle slopes between the hills
Low latitude (28 N): low sun lasts only minutes each day
Irrigated centre-pivot farms are spreading across the surrounding desert, so the bare surface may not stay untouched
black_desert.access: About 370 km by paved road from Cairo via Bahariya Oasis. Day trips by 4x4 are common.

gilf_kebir.why: A large sandstone plateau with steep scarps and cliffs, used here to test the steep end of the slope histogram.
works: Steep scarps and cliffs fill the high-slope bins
Bare, hyperarid desert
Isolated and unvisited, so the surface is undisturbed
breaks: Sandstone, not basalt or anorthosite
Erosional scarps, not impact rims
Low latitude (23 N): low sun lasts only minutes each day
gilf_kebir.access: Inside Gilf Kebir National Park. Needs military permits, an escort, and a multi-day 4x4 expedition from Dakhla or Kharga.
